title: Hidden in all beings
theme: This self, hidden in all beings, does not shine forth; it is seen by those who see the subtle, with a sharpened, subtle intellect.

words.context: Śaṅkara: «ब्रह्मादिस्तम्बपर्यन्तेषु», from Brahmā down to a tuft of grass
Śaṅkara: «आत्मत्वेन कस्यचित्», does not appear to anyone as his self
Śaṅkara derives it from agra, ‘point’ (agram iva), and explains it as one-pointed, «एकाग्रतयोपेतयेत्येतत्»
Śaṅkara: «सूक्ष्मवस्तुनिरूपणपरया», intent on discerning what is subtle

words.meaning: by those who see the subtle

sandhi.rule: The pronoun saḥ / eṣaḥ drops its visarga before any consonant.

sandhi.type: aḥ before ā, with the ā elided (Vedic)
sandhi.rule: As before a short a, the visarga becomes u and a + u give o, P. 6.1.87 (आद्गुणः); here the following long ā is also elided, as the avagraha shows. The ordinary rule would give गूढ आत्मा; every witness of this edition has the elided form, which keeps the pāda at eight syllables.
u becomes v before a dissimilar vowel, P. 6.1.77 (इको यणचि).

samasa.meaning: those whose habit is to see the subtle (Śaṅkara's analysis)

morphology.note: agrya, ‘at the point, foremost’, from agra with the suffix -ya. The base file of the Advaita Sharada text reads अग्न्यया here and in Śaṅkara's quotation; this edition corrects it to अग्र्यया with the other witnesses (corrections.json).
Present passive of √dṛś, ‘see’, built on the weak root form dṛś-; the agent stands in the instrumental (sūkṣmadarśibhiḥ).

translation.literal: This self, hidden in all beings, does not shine forth; but it is seen by those who see the subtle, with a sharp, subtle intellect.
translation.readable: Hidden in every being, this self does not show itself; but those who see what is subtle see it, with an intellect made sharp and fine.

anvaya: एषः आत्मा सर्वेषु भूतेषु गूढः [सन्] न प्रकाशते; सूक्ष्मदर्शिभिः तु अग्र्यया सूक्ष्मया बुद्ध्या दृश्यते ।
syntax: Two clauses set against each other by tu: an active clause with a negative (na prakāśate) and a passive clause (dṛśyate) whose agent is the instrumental plural sūkṣmadarśibhiḥ and whose means is the instrumental buddhyā with two adjectives.

ambiguities.topic: How can it be ‘seen’ if it ‘does not shine’?
ambiguities.note: Śaṅkara raises the contradiction with 1.2.22 (‘having known, the wise one does not grieve’) and answers that it does not shine for an untrained intellect: «असंस्कृतबुद्धेरविज्ञेयत्वान्न प्रकाशत इत्युक्तम्»; it is seen by a trained one.

Śaṅkara: by ignorance and māyā, so that no one takes it as his self — «अविद्यामायाच्छन्नः»; Raṅgarāmānuja: it does not shine for those who have not mastered their outer and inner faculties, «अजितबाह्यान्तःकरणानां, न यथावत् प्रकाशते».

metre.name: anuṣṭubh
metre.note: Anuṣṭubh, 2 × 16 (8 + 8), regular as written: gūḍho 'tmā has three syllables because the ā of ātmā is elided.

beginner: The ladder of the previous verses ended in the Person, the inmost reality. Now Death says why most people never notice it. It is hidden inside every living thing, so close that it does not stand out as something to look at. It does not shine forth by itself. Yet it can be seen, by people who have trained themselves to notice what is fine and subtle, using an intellect that has become sharp and steady, like the point of a needle. Śaṅkara says that what hides it is ignorance: people take the body and the senses for themselves, and do not take the self for themselves even when told. Raṅgarāmānuja says it does not show itself to those who have not mastered their senses and mind. The next verse says how that mastery is practised.
analogy: Like the thread inside a string of beads: it runs through every bead and holds them together, but one sees the beads, not the thread.

commentary.label: direct
commentary.text: The self is hidden in all beings and does not shine forth, but it is seen with a sharp and subtle intellect by those who see the subtle.

commentary.q: Śaṅkara: hidden by ignorance, seen by the trained
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: The Person is hidden in all beings, covered by ignorance and māyā, «अविद्यामायाच्छन्नः», and so does not appear to anyone as his self. Śaṅkara marvels at this: «अहो अतिगम्भीरा दुरवगाह्या विचित्रा चेयं माया». It is seen by an intellect that is trained and one-pointed, «एकाग्रतयोपेतयेत्येतत्», and subtle, «सूक्ष्मवस्तुनिरूपणपरया», by those who have learned to see the subtle through the steps of 1.3.10–11.

commentary.q: Raṅgarāmānuja: present as the self of all
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: The self of this verse is the one present in all beings as their self, «सर्वेषु भूतेषु आत्मतया वर्तमानः»; it does not appear as it is to those who have not mastered their faculties, «अजितबाह्यान्तःकरणानां». It is seen with an intellect free of outer and inner activity, by the power that discerns subtle things: «सूक्ष्मार्थविवेचनशक्त्या».

commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: For the world's not seeing what is its own self, Śaṅkara cites the Gītā (7.25): «नाहं प्रकाशः सर्वस्य योगमायासमावृतः» — ‘I am not manifest to all, covered by yogamāyā’.

commentary.label: linguistic
commentary.text: The base file reads अग्न्यया, and its copy of Śaṅkara's bhāṣya repeats the slip. GRETIL, the vishvAsa mūla and Madhva's text read अग्र्यया, and Śaṅkara's own gloss, agram iva, ‘like a point’, points to agra, ‘point’; the edition corrects the text (corrections.json). The sandhi gūḍho 'tmā, with the long ā elided, is in every witness.

advaita.text: The self of all is hidden by ignorance and māyā — «अविद्यामायाच्छन्नः» — so that no one takes it for his own self; a one-pointed, subtle intellect sees it.

visistadvaita.text: The supreme Self dwells in all beings as their self, «सर्वेषु भूतेषु आत्मतया वर्तमानः», and is seen only by those whose outer and inner faculties are mastered.

schools.disagreement: What hides the self — ignorance and māyā, so that one's own identity with it is missed (Śaṅkara), or unmastered faculties, which keep the indwelling Lord from being perceived as he is (Raṅgarāmānuja). Madhva's bhāṣya, in our source, has no comment on this verse; his comment after 1.3.13 concerns 1.3.13.

parallels.note: The Muṇḍaka says the same of the self: not grasped by the eye or by speech, but seen by one whose nature is purified.

parallels.quote: तं दुर्दर्शं गूढमनुप्रविष्टं गुहाहितं गह्वरेष्ठं पुराणम्
parallels.note: The same word gūḍha, ‘hidden’, described the God hard to see in 1.2.12.

contemporary.text: What is always present is the hardest thing to notice: one hears the clock only when it stops. The verse says the self is hidden not because it is far but because it is everywhere, and that seeing it is a matter of a finer attention rather than a new object. This is a reflection, not a claim made by the text.

reflect.beginner: What is always with you that you almost never notice?
reflect.deeper: If the self is the one who sees, in what sense can it be ‘seen’? How do Śaṅkara and Raṅgarāmānuja each answer?
reflect.practice: For a few minutes, notice not what you are seeing but that seeing is going on.

flags.note: The sandhi gūḍho 'tmā (gūḍhaḥ + ātmā, with the long ā elided, Vedic) is in every witness; the checker's sandhi engine must accept it for this record's padaccheda to be proven.
What hides the self: ignorance and māyā (Śaṅkara) or unmastered faculties (Raṅgarāmānuja). Madhva's bhāṣya has no comment on the verse.
